survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The analysis uses OECD Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) microdata for adults aged 16–65, combined with country-level policy indicators. The paper reports logit regressions with robust standard errors and pooled cross-country specifications, but it does not document the use of PIAAC sampling weights or replicate weights in the provided text. Because the dependent variables are mismatch indicators derived from proficiency scores and self-reports, analysts would typically use PIAAC’s complex survey design weights when estimating population-representative effects; however, the manuscript does not specify any weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate method. The sample is restricted by the PIAAC waves included (first wave 2008–2013; second wave 2012–2016) and further excludes Indonesia, Singapore, and the Russian Federation in the empirical analysis, as stated in the text.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The study’s mismatch outcome is constructed from literacy proficiency scores and self-reported mismatch using OECD’s mismatch indicator approach, but the provided text does not describe whether proficiency is represented via plausible values (PV-based achievement) or via an alternative scoring/estimation approach. Because the paper does not report any explicit PV handling procedure and does not document how missing data were treated, the missing-data strategy is a reporting gap. This omission matters because PIAAC datasets typically contain item nonresponse and missing background variables, which can affect logit estimates if not handled transparently.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Uses OECD Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) for adults aged 16–65 in literacy, numeracy and problem solving in technology-rich environments. The mismatch indicator follows OECD (2013) and is based on combining self-reported mismatch with quantitative literacy proficiency, using occupation (1-digit ISCO) thresholds derived from well-matched workers (10th/90th percentiles as described). The empirical cross-country analysis includes countries from the first wave (2008–2013) and second wave (2012–2016), but explicitly excludes Indonesia, Singapore, and the Russian Federation from the empirical analysis. The paper also reports a New Zealand-specific baseline logit model using PIAAC 2015 data (as indicated in Table 1 source), and pooled cross-country regressions using Survey of Adult Skills (2012 and 2015) data.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD working paper uses the OECD Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) to construct a literacy-proficiency-based skills mismatch indicator that combines self-reported mismatch with quantitative proficiency thresholds by occupation (1-digit ISCO). It reports descriptive cross-country mismatch rates (e.g., New Zealand at 28% vs OECD average 25%, with over-skilling about 18% and under-skilling about 10% in New Zealand) and then estimates logit models for mismatch, over-skilling, and under-skilling using New Zealand baseline data (2015) and pooled cross-country regressions using PIAAC waves (2012 and 2015), excluding Indonesia, Singapore, and the Russian Federation. The paper’s policy results are expressed as marginal effects from logit regressions and scenario-based changes in mismatch probabilities, with pseudo-R2 values reported by policy panel. It does not report machine-learning model performance metrics because the empirical strategy is econometric (logit/OLS), and it also does not document plausible-value handling or missing-data procedures in the provided text, limiting transparency for replication.
